facts.claim: Amazon’s Linden, Smith and York (2003) report that clicks and sales from their personal recommendations vastly beat those from content shown to everyone, such as top-seller lists.
Resnick et al.’s GroupLens (1994) guessed which news articles a reader would like from other readers’ ratings, on the rule that people who agreed in the past will probably agree again.

Linden, Smith and York (2003) describe Amazon matching each product a customer bought to products customers tend to buy together, worked out ahead of time, so building a customer’s suggestions depends only on how many items they bought or rated, not on Amazon’s 29 million-plus customers.
Koren, Bell and Volinsky (IEEE Computer, 2009) write that, as the Netflix Prize showed, matrix factorization models beat classic nearest-neighbour methods at product recommendations.
The same article says factorization can also take in implicit feedback, changes over time and confidence levels.
Koren, Bell and Volinsky (2009) place users and products on, say, 20 to 100 factors found from rating patterns; in their Netflix tests, more factors predicted ratings more accurately.
Hu, Koren and Volinsky (ICDM 2008) treat implicit data, such as what people bought or watched, as signs of liking or not liking held with very different confidence.
Schein et al. (SIGIR 2002) call it the cold-start problem: a recommender that learns only from people’s ratings cannot suggest an item no one has rated yet, as it has no preference data to go on.
Chaney, Stewart and Engelhardt (RecSys 2018) note that recommenders are trained on data from users already shown recommendations, a feedback loop.
In their simulations, that loop makes users’ behaviour more alike without making them better off.
Covington, Adams and Sargin (RecSys 2016) describe YouTube’s recommender in two stages: one model picks candidates from the catalogue, a second model ranks them.
